checks.label: The voltage wave has a "head start" on the current wave; the voltage leads the current, and the current lags behind the voltage: on every screen each top and bottom of the drawn voltage comes a quarter cycle before the drawn current's
Inductive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_L = 2πfL. The drawn X_L line, its dot and the supply's peak ÷ the current's peak all agree with it at every setting of the frequency slider

Reactance in ohms for any inductor is directly proportional to the frequency of the alternating current: the drawn X_L line runs straight from zero, and twice the frequency gives twice the reactance and half the current

Power is never returned to the source by a resistive load, as it is with reactive loads: the coil's drawn power, the drawn voltage × the drawn current at each instant, goes below zero and averages zero, while the heater's never goes below zero
60 Hz is the most common frequency adopted for use on board ship: answered, the ship screen runs the coil at 60 Hz, where X_L is 12 Ω and the current peaks at 8.33 A
UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: the mains coil drawing 4 A has X_L = 230 ÷ 4 = 57.5 Ω at 50 Hz, and on a 230 V, 60 Hz supply 69 Ω and 3.33 A

The coil's voltage is its inductance × the steepness of its current: 100 V at 0 ms where the tangent is steepest, 0 V at 5 ms where it lies flat, −100 V at 10 ms; every drawn voltage point is L × the drawn current's slope there
At 0 ms the tangent is just as steep at every frequency, so the current peaks at 20 A on 25 Hz, 10 A on 50 Hz, 8.33 A on 60 Hz and 5 A on 100 Hz
On 50 Hz the coil's power rises to 500 W and dips to −500 W, two humps up and two down each 20 ms cycle
At 0 Hz, steady DC, X_L is 0 Ω and only the wire's 0.5 Ω is left: 100 V ÷ 0.5 Ω = 200 A
